I've also added a website for the plugin, at charts.datasette.io. The new website includes a tutorial for plugin authors, and a gallery showing all of the core charts and annotations, each one linking to an interactive demo on Datasette Lite.

items.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
items.content:
sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite

This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025. It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics.

Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO. In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck.

sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy!

It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync:

The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most.

Update: Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released.

Tags: backups, sqlite

items.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
items.content:
My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News.

I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that.

He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted.

The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too!

Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously.

(Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.)

items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
items.content:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Battledrones Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

It's good at 3D modeling, too. Here's the "Goliath" mech from my Battledrones game, as seen in the model viewer debug tool:

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

items.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
items.content:
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery

Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.

Here's the digitized sketchbook.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.

Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

Tags: history, ai, generative-ai, llms, ai-assisted-search, deep-blue, gpt-6-astra

items.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
items.content:
GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.

GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights:

We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening.

I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.

It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.

I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.

Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one:

I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.

It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.

I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

items.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
items.content:
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS.

This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!

I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):

Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude):

Ladybird (72925)  [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926)  [61 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (72927)  [29 MB]
    ├── ProcessReaper (72928)  [1 MB]
    ├── Compositor (72930)  [123 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (72953)  [36 MB]
    ├── WebContent (72984)  [819 MB]
    ├── MediaServer (73006)  [118 MB]
    ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007)  [20 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73052)  [144 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73057)  [73 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73073)  [166 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73094)  [70 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73112)  [116 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (73113)  [27 MB]
    └── WebContent (73185)  [60 MB]

Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).

I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool. It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.

The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite, which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:

undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')

I filed an issue about this, then found a FIXME annotation in the source code.

The October explosion

The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI, describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.

Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months:

That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.

This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark, they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari!

How did they do that? Coding agents:

Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing.

I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.

Should you use Ladybird?

Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser:

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.

I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

items.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
items.content:
Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0

I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin.

You can try it out in Datasette Lite here. It looks like this:

The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3, Observable Plot, and topojson-client), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows.

Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch.

As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others.

The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account. Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows.

The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set.

I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible.

items.title: Muru
items.content:
Muru

Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.

Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.

As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.

Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:

  • 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next
  • 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru
  • 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers
  • 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together
  • 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many
  • 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development
  • 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together
  • 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice
  • 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts
  • 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh
  • 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container
  • 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it
  • 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report
  • 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero
  • 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule
  • 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding
  • 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page
  • 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar
  • 2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help

That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read:

The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.

items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.content:
Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)

Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.

In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.

I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.

Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.

Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.content:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

Via Lobste.rs

Tags: mysql, postgresql, replication, scaling, wikipedia, ai-security-research

A key new feature is the "WAIT FOR LSN" command, enabling "read-your-writes" consistency for applications reading from standbys. It allows sessions on a standby to wait for specific write-ahead log (WAL) replay before querying, ensuring data consistency. This feature is similar to Wikipedia's approach using MySQL replication. The release highlights improvements in replication and reliability.

items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.content:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

The pattern isolates agent code in a dedicated sandbox while keeping the agent outside, enhancing security against errors or prompt injection attacks. Three sandbox server implementations—external-sandbox-v86, external-sandbox-container, and external-sandbox-quicksand—are presented, all offering a common localhost API for integration with Pi, Claude Code, or Codex. items.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
items.content:
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.

You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:

  • Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script
  • Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI
  • Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository
  • Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette
  • Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools

The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.

As an example, consider the following URL:

https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:

That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.

Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:

https://lite.datasette.io/
  ?install=datasette-maplibre
  &url=https://.../demo.db
  &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
  #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins.

&url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.

&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.

#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23 is a URL-encoded #) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data.

That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year.

The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README.

I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:

Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty.

Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score

How this works, using service workers

Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.

The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML.

This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.

The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.

Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:

/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS)

Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about?

The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.

Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.

The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.

Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.

(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)

I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README:

This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!

Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite

I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite.

Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.

Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.

In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process.

WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.

datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this:

pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl

That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.

Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.

Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29)">this bonus tool for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1:

This should work for every other Python app, too

Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.

C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026.

One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.

I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.
